\section{Introduction}

Consider a finite list of symbols. Which of its features survive a consistent renaming of the
symbols? Exactly one: the record of \emph{which positions carry equal entries}. This record --- the
kernel, or equality pattern --- is the subject of this paper.

The idea is elementary and appears throughout mathematics and computer science, usually unnamed. In
model theory it is the type of a tuple in the pure theory of equality; in database theory it is the
equality pattern of a row; in symmetry reduction for model checking it is the canonical form used to
collapse states differing only in the identities of interchangeable components.

What is less commonly presented is a single development in which (i) the completeness of the
invariant, (ii) its computable normal form, (iii) its enumeration by the Bell numbers together with
the full Stirling refinement, and (iv) its use as an invariant of Diophantine equations, all appear
as consequences of one definition. That is what we do here. Throughout, $[n] = \{0,1,\dots,n-1\}$
and tuples are functions $f : [n] \to A$.

\section{Kernels and canonical forms}

\begin{definition}[Kernel]
For $f : [n] \to A$, the \emph{kernel} of $f$ is the relation $\Ker(f)$ on $[n]$ given by
$\Ker(f)(i,j) \iff f_i = f_j$.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}
$\Ker(f)$ is an equivalence relation on $[n]$, whose classes are the nonempty fibres of $f$
transported to the index set. For $f : [n] \to A$ and $g : [n] \to B$ one has $\Ker(f) = \Ker(g)$
if and only if $f_i = f_j \iff g_i = g_j$ for all $i,j$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity are those of equality in $A$; the second statement is the
pointwise reading of equality of relations.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Invariance]\label{prop:inv}
If $\sigma : A \to B$ is injective then $\Ker(\sigma \circ f) = \Ker(f)$. In particular $\Ker$ is a
$\Sym(A)$-invariant for the action of $\Sym(A)$ on $A^{[n]}$ by post-composition.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
$\sigma(f_i) = \sigma(f_j)$ implies $f_i = f_j$ by injectivity, and conversely by applying $\sigma$.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Canonical form]
Let $A$ have decidable equality. For $f : [n] \to A$ set
\[
  \canon(f)_i \;=\; \min\{\, j \in [n] : f_j = f_i \,\},
\]
the least index in the fibre of $i$.
\end{definition}

Thus $\canon(f)$ labels each block of the kernel partition by its least element:
$(\mathrm{b},\mathrm{r},\mathrm{g},\mathrm{b},\mathrm{r}) \mapsto (0,1,2,0,1)$ and
$(7,7,4,7,4) \mapsto (0,0,2,0,2)$.

\begin{proposition}[Calculus of $\canon$]\label{prop:calc}
For all $f,g$ and all $i,j$:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item $f_{\canon(f)_i} = f_i$ and $\canon(f)_i \le i$;
  \item $\canon(f)_i = c$ iff $f_c = f_i$ and $c \le j$ for every $j$ with $f_j = f_i$;
  \item $f_i = f_j \iff \canon(f)_i = \canon(f)_j$; hence $\Ker(\canon(f)) = \Ker(f)$;
  \item $\canon(f) = \canon(g) \iff \Ker(f) = \Ker(g)$;
  \item $\canon$ is idempotent: $\canon(\canon(f)) = \canon(f)$;
  \item if $\sigma$ is injective then $\canon(\sigma\circ f) = \canon(f)$;
  \item if $f$ is injective then $\canon(f) = \mathrm{id}$, the \emph{discrete} pattern.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
(1) and (2) are immediate from the definition of a least element. (3): if $f_i = f_j$ the two fibres
coincide, hence so do their minima; conversely apply $f$ and use (1). (4): forward by (3) on both
sides; conversely $\canon(g)_i$ is verified to be a least element for $f$. (5) is (4) with
$g = \canon(f)$, using (3). (6) is (4) with Proposition~\ref{prop:inv}. (7): injectivity makes each
fibre a singleton.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Patterns]
$P_n$ is the set of tuples $p : [n] \to [n]$ with $\canon(p) = p$, equivalently the image of
$\canon$. Its elements are the \emph{patterns of length $n$}, classically the \emph{restricted
growth strings}: $p_0 = 0$ and $p_i \le 1 + \max_{j<i}p_j$.
\end{definition}

\section{The completeness theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Completeness]\label{thm:complete}
Let $B$ be a finite set with decidable equality and $f,g : [n] \to B$. Then
\[
  \bigl(\exists\,\sigma \in \Sym(B),\ \sigma\circ f = g\bigr)
  \iff \Ker(f) = \Ker(g) \iff \canon(f) = \canon(g).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Left to right is Proposition~\ref{prop:inv}. Conversely assume $f_i = f_j \iff g_i = g_j$ for all
$i,j$. Define $e : \im(f) \to \im(g)$ by choosing, for $x \in \im(f)$, an index $i$ with $f_i = x$
and setting $e(x) = g_i$; the hypothesis makes this independent of the choice. The symmetric
construction is inverse to it, so $e$ is a bijection $\im(f) \to \im(g)$. Since $B$ is finite the
complements of the two images are equinumerous, so $e$ extends to $\sigma \in \Sym(B)$, and
$\sigma(f_i) = g_i$ for all $i$. The last equivalence is Proposition~\ref{prop:calc}(4).
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
Finiteness is used only for the extension step. Over an infinite alphabet the statement holds under
the extra hypothesis that the complements of the two images are equinumerous.
\end{remark}

\begin{corollary}[Effective classification]
Orbit equivalence of tuples over a finite alphabet is decided by computing and comparing two
canonical forms; no search over $|B|!$ permutations is required.
\end{corollary}

\section{Enumeration: patterns are counted by the Bell numbers}

Let $B_n$ be defined by $B_0 = 1$ and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:bell}
  B_{n+1} = \sum_{i=0}^{n}\binom{n}{i}B_{n-i}.
\end{equation}

\begin{theorem}[Bell enumeration]\label{thm:bell}
For every $n \ge 0$, $|P_n| = B_n$. Equivalently, for every finite index set $I$ the number of
equivalence relations on $I$ (equivalently, of set partitions of $I$) is $B_{|I|}$. The first values
are $1,1,2,5,15,52$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Let $K(I)$ be the number of equivalence relations on $I$ and $K(n) = K([n])$.

\emph{Step 1.} Sending a pattern $p$ to the relation $i \sim j \iff p_i = p_j$ is a bijection from
$P_n$ onto equivalence relations on $[n]$: a pattern is recovered as the least-element labelling of
its relation. Hence $|P_n| = K(n)$.

\emph{Step 2.} $K(I)$ depends only on $|I|$, since a bijection $I \to J$ conjugates equivalence
relations bijectively.

\emph{Step 3.} With $I^+ = I \sqcup \{\star\}$, an equivalence relation on $I^+$ is the same data as
a subset $s \subseteq I$ (the points equivalent to $\star$) together with an equivalence relation on
$I \setminus s$; the gluing and restriction constructions are mutually inverse. Hence
$K(I^+) = \sum_{s\subseteq I} K(I\setminus s)$.

\emph{Step 4.} Grouping the subsets by cardinality and using Step 2 gives
$K(n+1) = \sum_{k=0}^n \binom{n}{k}K(n-k)$, i.e.\ \eqref{eq:bell}. With $K(0)=1$, strong induction
gives $K(n) = B_n$.
\end{proof}

\section{The Stirling refinement}

\begin{definition}
For $p \in P_n$ let $\nb(p)$ be the number of distinct values of $p$ (the number of blocks), so
$\nb(p) \le n$, and set $S(n,k) = \#\{p \in P_n : \nb(p) = k\}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[Row sums]
$\sum_{k=0}^{n} S(n,k) = |P_n| = B_n$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proposition}[Boundary values]
$S(n,k) = 0$ for $k>n$; $S(n,n) = 1$; $S(0,0) = 1$; $S(n+1,0) = 0$; $S(n+1,1) = 1$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{theorem}[Stirling recursion]\label{thm:rec}
For all $n,k \ge 0$, $\; S(n+1,k+1) = S(n,k) + (k+1)\,S(n,k+1)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Split patterns of length $n+1$ with $k+1$ blocks by whether the last position is a singleton block.
If it is, deleting it is a bijection onto patterns of length $n$ with $k$ blocks (restriction and
extension-by-a-fresh-label are mutually inverse and preserve patterns). If it is not, the
restriction is a pattern of length $n$ with $k+1$ blocks and the extra datum is which of its $k+1$
blocks the new point joins, a $(k+1)$-to-one correspondence. Adding the two counts gives the
identity.
\end{proof}

For example $S(5,3) = S(4,2) + 3S(4,3) = 7 + 18 = 25$.

\begin{theorem}[Two blocks]\label{thm:two}
$S(n+1,2) = 2^n - 1$; consequently $2^n \le B_{n+1}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
A two-block pattern of length $n+1$ is determined by the block containing position $0$, which may be
any subset containing $0$ other than everything: $2^n - 1$ choices. The bound follows from
$B_{n+1} \ge S(n+1,1) + S(n+1,2)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Subdiagonals]
$S(n+1,n) = \binom{n+1}{2}$ and $S(n+2,n) = \binom{n+2}{3} + 3\binom{n+2}{4}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The first is induction from Theorem~\ref{thm:rec} and Pascal's rule; combinatorially, such a pattern
merges exactly one pair of positions. The second is induction from the first together with the
arithmetic identity $3\binom{n+2}{3} = n\binom{n+2}{2}$; combinatorially, two defects mean either
one block of size $3$ or two blocks of size $2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Columns $k = 3,4,5$]
For all $n \ge 0$,
\[
  6S(n,3) = 3^n - 3\cdot 2^n + 3,\qquad
  24S(n,4) = 4^n - 4\cdot 3^n + 6\cdot 2^n - 4,
\]
\[
  120S(n,5) = 5^n - 5\cdot 4^n + 10\cdot 3^n - 10\cdot 2^n + 5 .
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Induction on $n$, feeding the previous column into Theorem~\ref{thm:rec}; the base case is
$S(n,k) = 0$ for $k > n$. These are the inclusion--exclusion formulas
$k!\,S(n,k) = \sum_j (-1)^j\binom{k}{j}(k-j)^n$ for $k \le 5$, here obtained without
inclusion--exclusion.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
$B_6 = 203$, $B_7 = 877$, $B_8 = 4140$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[Fibre size]\label{thm:fibre}
Let $|B| = m$ and $p \in P_n$ with $\nb(p) = k$. The number of tuples $f : [n] \to B$ with
$\canon(f) = p$ is the falling factorial $m^{\underline{k}} = m(m-1)\cdots(m-k+1)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Such an $f$ is exactly $p$ followed by an injection from the $k$ blocks into $B$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Falling-factorial expansion]
$m^n = \sum_{k=0}^{n} S(n,k)\,m^{\underline{k}}$ for all $n,m \ge 0$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Count $B^{[n]}$ by the fibres of $\canon$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:fibre}) and group patterns by block
count.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Surjection count]
The number of surjections $[n] \to [k]$ is $k!\,S(n,k)$; in particular the number of surjections
$[n]\to[n]$ is $n!$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
A map onto $[k]$ is surjective iff its pattern has $k$ blocks, and each such fibre has
$k^{\underline{k}} = k!$ elements by Theorem~\ref{thm:fibre}. For $k = n$ the pattern is forced to be
discrete and $S(n,n) = 1$.
\end{proof}

\section{Orbit counting over arbitrary alphabets}

\begin{theorem}[Large alphabet]
If $|B| \ge n$, the number of orbits of $\Sym(B)$ on $B^{[n]}$ is $B_n$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
By Theorem~\ref{thm:complete} the map $f \mapsto \canon(f)$ descends to an injection from orbits into
$P_n$; by Theorem~\ref{thm:fibre} every pattern is realised since $k \le n \le |B|$. Apply
Theorem~\ref{thm:bell}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Arbitrary alphabet]
For any finite $B$, the number of orbits of $\Sym(B)$ on $B^{[n]}$ is $\sum_{k=0}^{|B|}S(n,k)$,
which equals $B_n$ when $|B| \ge n$ and is strictly smaller when $|B| < n$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The canonical form is a bijection from orbits onto the patterns with at most $|B|$ blocks: a tuple
over $B$ has at most $|B|$ distinct entries, and conversely every pattern with $k \le |B|$ blocks is
realised. If $|B| < n$ the term $S(n,n) = 1$ is missing from the sum.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Sharpness]
If $|B| < n$ then no $f : [n] \to B$ has the discrete pattern, since the image of $\canon(f)$ has at
most $|B|$ elements while the identity has image of size $n$.
\end{proposition}

\section{Growth and congruences for the Bell numbers}

\begin{theorem}[Monotonicity]
$B_n < B_{n+1}$ for $n \ge 1$ and $B_n \le B_{n+1}$ for all $n$; hence $B$ is monotone, strictly
monotone on $[1,\infty)$, and $n \le B_n$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Appending a fresh singleton block injects $P_n$ into $P_{n+1}$; the constant pattern of length $n+1$
is not in the image once $n \ge 1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Super-multiplicativity]\label{thm:super}
$B_mB_n \le B_{m+n}$ for all $m,n$, strictly if $m,n \ge 1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
For equivalence relations $r$ on $A$ and $s$ on $C$, let $r \oplus s$ on $A \sqcup C$ relate two
points iff they lie in the same summand and are related there. Then $(r,s)\mapsto r\oplus s$ is
injective (restrict to each summand), giving the inequality. If both summands are nonempty, the
total relation on $A \sqcup C$ is not of this form, so the injection is not onto.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
$B_n^k \le B_{nk}$ for all $n,k$; in particular $2^k = B_2^k \le B_{2k}$. Already
$B_2B_2 = 4 < 15 = B_4$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[Touchard's congruence]\label{thm:touchard}
For every prime $p$ and every $n \ge 0$, $\; B_{p+n} \equiv B_{n+1} + B_n \pmod p$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Let $X$ be the set of equivalence relations on $\mathbb{Z}/p \sqcup [n]$, so $|X| = B_{p+n}$ by
Theorem~\ref{thm:bell}. The cyclic group $C_p$ acts by rotating the left summand and fixing the
right one. For a group of prime order $p$ every orbit has size $1$ or $p$, so
$|X| \equiv |X^{C_p}| \pmod p$. Now classify the invariant relations by the block $\beta$ of the left
point $0$. If $\beta$ contains another left point $d \ne 0$, invariance under rotation by $d$ and
chaining (using that $d$ generates $\mathbb{Z}/p$) collapse all left points into one block; what
remains is an equivalence relation on $[n] \sqcup \{\star\}$, where $\star$ is the merged block:
$B_{n+1}$ possibilities. Otherwise every left point is a singleton block unrelated to the right
summand, leaving an arbitrary relation on $[n]$: $B_n$ possibilities. Hence
$|X^{C_p}| = B_{n+1}+B_n$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
$B_p \equiv 2 \pmod p$ for every prime $p$; e.g.\ $B_7 = 877 = 7\cdot 125 + 2$. Taking $p=5$, $n=3$
gives $B_8 \equiv B_4 + B_3 = 20 \equiv 0 \pmod 5$, consistent with $B_8 = 4140 = 5\cdot 828$.
\end{corollary}

\section{Kernel spectra of Diophantine equations}

\begin{definition}[Kernel spectrum]
For an equation $E$ in $n$ unknowns over $\mathbb{N}$ with solution set $\mathcal S(E)$, put
$\Spec(E) = \{\canon(t) : t \in \mathcal S(E)\} \subseteq P_n$, and call $B_n - |\Spec(E)|$ its
\emph{defect}.
\end{definition}

For $n = 3$ the $B_3 = 5$ patterns are $(0,1,2)$ (discrete), $(0,1,1)$, $(0,1,0)$, $(0,0,0)$ and
$(0,0,2)$ (equal legs).

\begin{lemma}[Square multiplier]\label{lem:sq}
If $k,a,c \in \mathbb{N}$, $a \ne 0$ and $ka^2 = c^2$, then $k$ is a perfect square. Conversely if
$k = m^2$ then $k\cdot 1^2 = m^2$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Let $g = \gcd(a,c)$, $a = ga'$, $c = gc'$ with $\gcd(a',c') = 1$. Cancelling $g^2$ gives
$ka'^2 = c'^2$, so $a'^2 \mid c'^2$ while being coprime to it; hence $a' = 1$ and $k = c'^2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
$2a^2 = c^2$ has no solution with $a \ne 0$, since $2$ is not a perfect square.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[Pythagorean kernel spectrum]
A pattern $p \in P_3$ is the kernel of a solution of $a^2+b^2=c^2$ over $\mathbb{N}$ if and only if
$p \ne (0,0,2)$. Hence
$\Spec = \{(0,1,2),(0,1,1),(0,1,0),(0,0,0)\}$ has $4 = B_3 - 1$ elements: the Pythagorean cone is
kernel-deficient of defect exactly one.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
If $\canon(t) = (0,0,2)$ then $t_0 = t_1$ and $t_2 \ne t_0$, so $2t_0^2 = t_2^2$; $t_0 \ne 0$
contradicts Lemma~\ref{lem:sq}, and $t_0 = 0$ forces $t_2 = 0 = t_0$. The other four patterns are
realised by $(3,4,5)$, $(0,1,1)$, $(1,0,1)$ and $(0,0,0)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}
Every Pythagorean triple with all entries strictly positive has the discrete pattern: the legs
cannot be equal, and a leg equal to the hypotenuse forces the other leg to vanish.
\end{proposition}

\begin{theorem}[Equal-legs criterion]
For $k \ge 0$, the equation $\sum_{i<k}x_i^2 = y^2$ has a solution with all $x_i$ equal to a common
nonzero value if and only if $k$ is a perfect square. In particular this is impossible for $k = 2$
and $k = 3$ and possible for $k = 4$, via $1^2+1^2+1^2+1^2 = 2^2$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Setting all legs to $a$ gives $ka^2 = y^2$; apply Lemma~\ref{lem:sq} in both directions.
\end{proof}

For an exponent $p$ let $\Spec(p)$ be the kernel spectrum of $x^p + y^p = z^p$ over $\mathbb{N}$.

\begin{lemma}[$2$-adic obstruction]\label{lem:2adic}
For $p \ge 2$ and $a \ne 0$ one has $2a^p \ne c^p$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Both sides are nonzero; comparing the exponent of $2$ gives $1 + p\,v_2(a) = p\,v_2(c)$, hence
$p \mid 1$, impossible.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
For every $p \ge 2$ the equal-legs pattern is not in $\Spec(p)$, so $\Spec(p) \subseteq \Spec(2)$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proposition}
For every $p \ge 1$ the patterns $(0,1,1)$, $(0,1,0)$, $(0,0,0)$ lie in $\Spec(p)$, realised by
$(0,1,1)$, $(1,0,1)$, $(0,0,0)$. Moreover $\Spec(1) = P_3$, since $1+1=2$ realises the equal-legs
pattern and $3+4=7$ the discrete one.
\end{proposition}

\begin{theorem}[Discrete pattern equals positive solvability]\label{thm:disc}
For $p \ge 2$, the discrete pattern lies in $\Spec(p)$ if and only if there exist $x,y,z>0$ with
$x^p+y^p=z^p$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Given a positive solution, $x \ne y$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:2adic} and $x \ne z$, $y \ne z$ since the other
leg is positive; so the triple is injective and its pattern is discrete. Conversely a Fermat triple
with distinct entries has all entries positive: a vanishing leg forces the other leg to equal the
hypotenuse.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Kernel-theoretic Fermat's Last Theorem]
Let $p \ge 2$. Then $|\Spec(p)| = 3$ iff $x^p+y^p=z^p$ has no solution with $x,y,z>0$, and
$|\Spec(p)| = 4$ iff it has one. In the first case
$\Spec(p) = \{(0,1,1),(0,1,0),(0,0,0)\}$; in the second,
$\Spec(p) = \{(0,1,2),(0,1,1),(0,1,0),(0,0,0)\}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The spectrum lies inside the four-element Pythagorean spectrum and contains the three degenerate
patterns; the only question is whether the discrete pattern belongs, which Theorem~\ref{thm:disc}
settles.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
$|\Spec(2)| = 4$, witnessed by $(3,4,5)$; and for $p \ge 3$, $|\Spec(p)| = 3$ --- Fermat's Last
Theorem in the form ``the kernel spectrum of the Fermat equation of exponent $p \ge 3$ omits the
discrete pattern''.
\end{corollary}

\section{Algorithms}

\paragraph{Canonicalisation.} Computing $\canon(f)$ naively costs $O(n^2)$ comparisons; with a hash
map from values to first occurrence it is $O(n)$ expected time and $O(n)$ space. Orbit equivalence is
then decided in linear time.

\paragraph{Pattern enumeration.} Patterns are exactly the restricted growth strings, generated by
depth-first search extending a prefix of maximum label $m$ by any of $0,\dots,m+1$: no rejection,
$O(nB_n)$ time, $O(n)$ space.

\paragraph{Tables.} Iterating the recursion of Theorem~\ref{thm:rec} fills the $n \times n$ block-count
triangle in $O(n^2)$ integer operations; row sums give the Bell numbers, e.g.\ $B_8 = 4140$ without
touching the $4140$ objects counted.

\paragraph{Kernel spectra.} Enumerate the $B_n$ patterns; for each, substitute one variable per block
and decide whether the reduced equation has a solution with block-variables pairwise distinct. All
arithmetic difficulty is concentrated in finitely many reduced Diophantine problems.

\section{Discussion and future directions}

Three features distinguish kernel patterns: \emph{completeness} over finite alphabets;
\emph{computability}, the invariant being a short integer tuple; and \emph{exact enumeration}, the
invariant's own state space being the Bell numbers refined by the block-count triangle. Once
$S(n,k)$ is defined as a count of patterns, the recursion, closed forms, falling-factorial
expansion, surjection count, super-multiplicativity and Touchard's congruence are all consequences
of manipulating patterns rather than formulas; Touchard's congruence in particular follows from a
single application of the orbit--fixed-point congruence for a cyclic group of prime order.

Applications include symmetry reduction (the orbit count over an arbitrary alphabet quantifies the
compression from $|B|^n$ states to $\sum_{k\le|B|}S(n,k)$), pseudonymised data (the kernel is exactly what survives renaming of field
values), and Diophantine bookkeeping, where the spectrum is faithful enough to encode positive
solvability exactly.

Open directions:

\begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{Log-concavity and unimodality.} Prove $S(n,k)^2 \ge S(n,k-1)S(n,k+1)$ for
  $1 \le k < n$, hence unimodality of each row with peak near $n/\log n$; combined with the row-sum
  identity this would upgrade the super-multiplicative bounds to the true growth order
  $B_n = n^{n(1+o(1))/\log n}$.
  \item \textbf{Higher congruences.} Extend Touchard's congruence to prime powers, e.g.\
  $B_{p^m+n} \equiv mB_n + B_{n+1} \pmod p$, and study the period of the Bell numbers modulo $p$
  (conjecturally $(p^p-1)/(p-1)$) with the same cyclic-action machinery.
  \item \textbf{Higher-arity spectra.} Compute the spectra of $\sum_{i<k}x_i^m = y^m$ for all $k,m$,
  generalising both the equal-legs criterion and the $2$-adic obstruction.
  \item \textbf{Spectral rigidity.} Determine which subsets of $P_n$ arise as kernel spectra of
  polynomial equations over $\mathbb{N}$; the question is open already for $n = 3$.
  \item \textbf{Stabilisation heights.} For a fixed equation, study how fast the spectrum stabilises
  as a height bound grows, and whether the stabilisation height is effectively boundable.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Conclusion}

The equality pattern of a tuple is the exact residue of the tuple under renaming of its entries: a

# 1. Canonical form and completeness of the invariant
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def canon(tup: Sequence[object]) -> Tuple[int, ...]:
    """Least-element labelling: canon(f)[i] = min{ j : f[j] == f[i] }.

    Linear time and space: scan left to right, recording the first occurrence
    index of each value.
    """
    first: Dict[object, int] = {}
    out: List[int] = []
    for i, x in enumerate(tup):
        if x not in first:
            first[x] = i
        out.append(first[x])
    return tuple(out)


def nblocks(pattern: Sequence[int]) -> int:
    """Number of blocks (distinct labels) of a pattern."""
    return len(set(pattern))


def same_orbit_by_search(f: Sequence[int], g: Sequence[int], alphabet_size: int) -> bool:
    """Brute force: is there a permutation sigma of the alphabet with sigma(f) = g?

    Exponential in the alphabet size; used only to validate the linear-time test.
    """
    from itertools import permutations

    for sigma in permutations(range(alphabet_size)):
        if tuple(sigma[x] for x in f) == tuple(g):
            return True
    return False

def patterns(n: int) -> Iterator[Tuple[int, ...]]:
    """Enumerate the patterns of length n, in least-element labelling.

    The restricted growth strings (p[0] = 0 and p[i] <= 1 + max(p[0..i-1])) are
    generated with no rejection, then relabelled by `canon` so that each block
    carries the index of its own least element.  Cost O(n * B_n) time, O(n) space.
    """
    if n == 0:
        yield ()
        return
    prefix: List[int] = [0]

    def extend(maximum: int) -> Iterator[Tuple[int, ...]]:
        if len(prefix) == n:
            yield canon(prefix)
            return
        for label in range(maximum + 2):
            prefix.append(label)
            yield from extend(max(maximum, label))
            prefix.pop()

    yield from extend(0)


def bell_numbers(upto: int) -> List[int]:
    """Bell numbers via the binomial recursion B_{n+1} = sum_i C(n,i) B_{n-i}."""
    bell = [1]
    for n in range(upto):
        bell.append(sum(comb(n, i) * bell[n - i] for i in range(n + 1)))
    return bell

def stirling_by_enumeration(n: int, k: int) -> int:
    """S(n,k) defined combinatorially: patterns of length n with exactly k blocks."""
    return sum(1 for p in patterns(n) if nblocks(p) == k)


def stirling_table(upto: int) -> List[List[int]]:
    """Fill the triangle with the recursion S(n+1,k+1) = S(n,k) + (k+1) S(n,k+1).

    O(upto^2) integer operations.
    """
    table = [[0] * (upto + 1) for _ in range(upto + 1)]
    table[0][0] = 1
    for n in range(upto):
        for k in range(upto):
            table[n + 1][k + 1] = table[n][k] + (k + 1) * table[n][k + 1]
    return table

def falling_factorial(m: int, k: int) -> int:
    """m^(k) = m (m-1) ... (m-k+1)."""
    result = 1
    for i in range(k):
        result *= max(m - i, 0) if m - i > 0 else 0
    return result if m >= k else 0

def demo_touchard(upto: int = 24) -> None:

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 8. Kernel spectra of Diophantine equations
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def pythagorean_spectrum(bound: int = 60) -> Set[Tuple[int, ...]]:
    """Patterns realised by solutions of a^2 + b^2 = c^2 with entries <= bound."""
    found: Set[Tuple[int, ...]] = set()
    for a in range(bound + 1):
        for b in range(bound + 1):
            s = a * a + b * b
            c = isqrt(s)
            if c * c == s and c <= bound:
                found.add(canon((a, b, c)))
    return found


def fermat_spectrum(p: int, bound: int = 60) -> Set[Tuple[int, ...]]:
    """Patterns realised by solutions of x^p + y^p = z^p with entries <= bound."""
    powers = {x ** p: x for x in range(bound + 1)}
    found: Set[Tuple[int, ...]] = set()
    for x in range(bound + 1):
        for y in range(bound + 1):
            s = x ** p + y ** p
            z = powers.get(s)
            if z is not None:
                found.add(canon((x, y, z)))
    return found


def equal_legs_dimension(k: int, bound: int = 200) -> Tuple[bool, Tuple[int, int] | None]:
    """Does sum_{i<k} a^2 = y^2 have a solution with a != 0?  (Theory: iff k is a square.)"""
    for a in range(1, bound + 1):
        s = k * a * a
        y = isqrt(s)
        if y * y == s:
            return True, (a, y)
    return False, None


def demo_spectra(bound: int = 60) -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("7. KERNEL SPECTRA OF DIOPHANTINE EQUATIONS")
    print("=" * 74)
    names = {
        (0, 1, 2): "discrete   (all distinct)",
        (0, 1, 1): "legs differ, b = c",
        (0, 1, 0): "a = c, b differs",
        (0, 0, 0): "all equal",
        (0, 0, 2): "EQUAL LEGS a = b, c differs",
    }
    all_patterns = list(patterns(3))

    spec = pythagorean_spectrum(bound)
    print(f"  a^2 + b^2 = c^2 with entries <= {bound}:")
    for pat in all_patterns:
        mark = "realised    " if pat in spec else "NOT realised"
        witness = ""
        if pat == (0, 1, 2):
            witness = "  e.g. (3,4,5)"
        if pat == (0, 0, 2):
            witness = "  (would need 2a^2 = c^2, impossible: 2 is not a square)"
        print(f"    {pat} {names[pat]:<28} {mark}{witness}")
    print(f"    |spectrum| = {len(spec)} = B_3 - 1 = 4   -> defect one")

    print("\n  equal legs in dimension k:  sum_{i<k} a^2 = y^2 with a != 0")
    print("    (theory: solvable iff k is a perfect square)")
    for k in range(1, 10):
        ok, witness = equal_legs_dimension(k)
        square = isqrt(k) ** 2 == k
        assert ok == square, k
        w = f"  witness a={witness[0]}, y={witness[1]}" if witness else ""
        print(f"    k={k}: solvable {str(ok):5s} | k a perfect square: {str(square):5s}{w}")

    print(f"\n  x^p + y^p = z^p with entries <= {bound}:")
    for p in range(1, 6):
        spec_p = fermat_spectrum(p, bound)
        pats = sorted(spec_p)
        note = ""
        if p == 1:
            note = "  all five patterns (1+1=2 gives equal legs)"
        elif p == 2:
            note = "  four patterns (3,4,5 gives the discrete one)"
        else:
            note = "  three patterns: discrete missing <=> no positive solution"
        print(f"    p={p}: |spectrum| = {len(spec_p)}  {pats}{note}")
    print("\n  For p >= 3 the discrete pattern is realised iff x^p + y^p = z^p has a")
    print("  positive solution, so its absence is exactly Fermat's Last Theorem at p.")
    print()


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def main() -> None:
    print()
    print("KERNEL PATTERNS -- NUMERICAL DEMONSTRATIONS")
    print()
    demo_completeness()
    demo_bell()
    demo_stirling()
    demo_fibres()
    demo_growth()
    demo_touchard()
    demo_spectra()
    print("All demonstrations completed; every assertion above verified numerically.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

        by_canon = canon(f) == canon(g)
        by_search = same_orbit_by_search(f, g, m)
        flag = "OK" if by_canon == by_search else "MISMATCH"
        print(
            f"  f={f}  g={g} | canon(f)={canon(f)} canon(g)={canon(g)}"
            f" -> same orbit? canon-test {by_canon}, brute force {by_search}  [{flag}]"
        )

    # Exhaustive check of the completeness theorem for all tuples.
    bad = 0
    for f in product(range(m), repeat=n):
        for g in product(range(m), repeat=n):
            if (canon(f) == canon(g)) != same_orbit_by_search(f, g, m):
                bad += 1
    print(f"  exhaustive check over all {m ** n}^2 pairs: {bad} disagreements (expected 0)")
    print()

# 2. Enumeration of patterns; Bell numbers
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def patterns(n: int) -> Iterator[Tuple[int, ...]]:
    """Enumerate the patterns of length n, in least-element labelling.

    The restricted growth strings (p[0] = 0 and p[i] <= 1 + max(p[0..i-1])) are
    generated with no rejection, then relabelled by `canon` so that each block
    carries the index of its own least element.  Cost O(n * B_n) time, O(n) space.
    """
    if n == 0:
        yield ()
        return
    prefix: List[int] = [0]

    def extend(maximum: int) -> Iterator[Tuple[int, ...]]:
        if len(prefix) == n:
            yield canon(prefix)
            return
        for label in range(maximum + 2):
            prefix.append(label)
            yield from extend(max(maximum, label))
            prefix.pop()

    yield from extend(0)


def bell_numbers(upto: int) -> List[int]:
    """Bell numbers via the binomial recursion B_{n+1} = sum_i C(n,i) B_{n-i}."""
    bell = [1]
    for n in range(upto):
        bell.append(sum(comb(n, i) * bell[n - i] for i in range(n + 1)))
    return bell

def stirling_by_enumeration(n: int, k: int) -> int:
    """S(n,k) defined combinatorially: patterns of length n with exactly k blocks."""
    return sum(1 for p in patterns(n) if nblocks(p) == k)


def stirling_table(upto: int) -> List[List[int]]:
    """Fill the triangle with the recursion S(n+1,k+1) = S(n,k) + (k+1) S(n,k+1).

    O(upto^2) integer operations.
    """
    table = [[0] * (upto + 1) for _ in range(upto + 1)]
    table[0][0] = 1
    for n in range(upto):
        for k in range(upto):
            table[n + 1][k + 1] = table[n][k] + (k + 1) * table[n][k + 1]
    return table

def falling_factorial(m: int, k: int) -> int:
    """m^(k) = m (m-1) ... (m-k+1)."""
    result = 1
    for i in range(k):
        result *= max(m - i, 0) if m - i > 0 else 0
    return result if m >= k else 0

def pythagorean_spectrum(bound: int = 60) -> Set[Tuple[int, ...]]:
    """Patterns realised by solutions of a^2 + b^2 = c^2 with entries <= bound."""
    found: Set[Tuple[int, ...]] = set()
    for a in range(bound + 1):
        for b in range(bound + 1):
            s = a * a + b * b
            c = isqrt(s)
            if c * c == s and c <= bound:
                found.add(canon((a, b, c)))
    return found


def fermat_spectrum(p: int, bound: int = 60) -> Set[Tuple[int, ...]]:
    """Patterns realised by solutions of x^p + y^p = z^p with entries <= bound."""
    powers = {x ** p: x for x in range(bound + 1)}
    found: Set[Tuple[int, ...]] = set()
    for x in range(bound + 1):
        for y in range(bound + 1):
            s = x ** p + y ** p
            z = powers.get(s)
            if z is not None:
                found.add(canon((x, y, z)))
    return found


def equal_legs_dimension(k: int, bound: int = 200) -> Tuple[bool, Tuple[int, int] | None]:
    """Does sum_{i<k} a^2 = y^2 have a solution with a != 0?  (Theory: iff k is a square.)"""
    for a in range(1, bound + 1):
        s = k * a * a
        y = isqrt(s)
        if y * y == s:
            return True, (a, y)
    return False, None


def demo_spectra(bound: int = 60) -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("7. KERNEL SPECTRA OF DIOPHANTINE EQUATIONS")
    print("=" * 74)
    names = {
        (0, 1, 2): "discrete   (all distinct)",
        (0, 1, 1): "legs differ, b = c",
        (0, 1, 0): "a = c, b differs",
        (0, 0, 0): "all equal",
        (0, 0, 2): "EQUAL LEGS a = b, c differs",
    }
    all_patterns = list(patterns(3))

    spec = pythagorean_spectrum(bound)
    print(f"  a^2 + b^2 = c^2 with entries <= {bound}:")
    for pat in all_patterns:
        mark = "realised    " if pat in spec else "NOT realised"
        witness = ""
        if pat == (0, 1, 2):
            witness = "  e.g. (3,4,5)"
        if pat == (0, 0, 2):
            witness = "  (would need 2a^2 = c^2, impossible: 2 is not a square)"
        print(f"    {pat} {names[pat]:<28} {mark}{witness}")
    print(f"    |spectrum| = {len(spec)} = B_3 - 1 = 4   -> defect one")

    print("\n  equal legs in dimension k:  sum_{i<k} a^2 = y^2 with a != 0")
    print("    (theory: solvable iff k is a perfect square)")
    for k in range(1, 10):
        ok, witness = equal_legs_dimension(k)
        square = isqrt(k) ** 2 == k
        assert ok == square, k
        w = f"  witness a={witness[0]}, y={witness[1]}" if witness else ""
        print(f"    k={k}: solvable {str(ok):5s} | k a perfect square: {str(square):5s}{w}")

    print(f"\n  x^p + y^p = z^p with entries <= {bound}:")
    for p in range(1, 6):
        spec_p = fermat_spectrum(p, bound)
        pats = sorted(spec_p)
        note = ""
        if p == 1:
            note = "  all five patterns (1+1=2 gives equal legs)"

        else:
            note = "  three patterns: discrete missing <=> no positive solution"
        print(f"    p={p}: |spectrum| = {len(spec_p)}  {pats}{note}")
    print("\n  For p >= 3 the discrete pattern is realised iff x^p + y^p = z^p has a")
    print("  positive solution, so its absence is exactly Fermat's Last Theorem at p.")
    print()

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Dict, Hashable, List, Sequence, Tuple


def canonical_form(tup: Sequence[Hashable]) -> Tuple[int, ...]:
    """Return the least-element labelling canon(f)[i] = min { j : f[j] == f[i] }.

    One left-to-right scan, O(n) expected time and O(n) space with a hash map from
    values to first-occurrence indices.  The result is a restricted growth string in
    least-element form and is a complete invariant of the tuple modulo renaming of the
    alphabet symbols.
    """
    first_occurrence: Dict[Hashable, int] = {}
    labels: List[int] = []
    for index, value in enumerate(tup):
        if value not in first_occurrence:
            first_occurrence[value] = index
        labels.append(first_occurrence[value])
    return tuple(labels)


def blocks(tup: Sequence[Hashable]) -> List[List[int]]:
    """The kernel partition of the index set, as a list of blocks of indices."""
    grouped: Dict[int, List[int]] = {}
    for index, label in enumerate(canonical_form(tup)):
        grouped.setdefault(label, []).append(index)
    return [grouped[key] for key in sorted(grouped)]


def block_count(tup: Sequence[Hashable]) -> int:
    """Number of blocks of the kernel partition (distinct entries of the tuple)."""
    return len(set(tup))


def same_renaming_orbit(f: Sequence[Hashable], g: Sequence[Hashable]) -> bool:
    """Decide whether some permutation of the alphabet carries f to g.

    Correct by the completeness theorem: over a finite alphabet, two tuples are in the
    same orbit of the symmetric group acting by post-composition if and only if their
    canonical forms coincide.  Cost O(n); the naive alternative searches |B|! permutations.
    """
    return len(f) == len(g) and canonical_form(f) == canonical_form(g)


def realisable_over(tup_pattern: Sequence[int], alphabet_size: int) -> bool:
    """Is a given pattern realised by some tuple over an alphabet of the given size?

    True exactly when the pattern has at most `alphabet_size` blocks.
    """
    return len(set(tup_pattern)) <= alphabet_size

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Dict, Iterator, List, Tuple


def _to_least_element_form(rgs: List[int]) -> Tuple[int, ...]:
    """Relabel a restricted growth string so each block carries its least index."""
    representative: Dict[int, int] = {}
    out: List[int] = []
    for index, label in enumerate(rgs):
        if label not in representative:
            representative[label] = index
        out.append(representative[label])
    return tuple(out)


def enumerate_patterns(n: int) -> Iterator[Tuple[int, ...]]:
    """Yield every equality pattern of an n-tuple exactly once.

    A pattern is a restricted growth string: p[0] = 0 and p[i] <= 1 + max(p[0..i-1]).
    Depth-first extension of a prefix whose largest label is `maximum` by any label in
    0, ..., maximum + 1 generates each pattern once with no rejected candidates, so the
    total cost is O(n * B_n) time (optimal up to output size) and O(n) working space.
    """
    if n == 0:
        yield ()
        return
    prefix: List[int] = []

    def extend(maximum: int) -> Iterator[Tuple[int, ...]]:
        if len(prefix) == n:
            yield _to_least_element_form(prefix)
            return
        for label in range(maximum + 2):
            prefix.append(label)
            yield from extend(max(maximum, label))
            prefix.pop()

    yield from extend(-1)


def count_patterns(n: int) -> int:
    """Number of patterns of length n; equals the Bell number B_n."""
    return sum(1 for _ in enumerate_patterns(n))


def count_patterns_by_blocks(n: int) -> Dict[int, int]:
    """Refine the count by number of blocks: the Stirling numbers of the second kind."""
    counts: Dict[int, int] = {}
    for pattern in enumerate_patterns(n):
        k = len(set(pattern))
        counts[k] = counts.get(k, 0) + 1
    return dict(sorted(counts.items()))

def stirling_triangle(nmax: int) -> List[List[int]]:
    """Fill S(n,k) for 0 <= n,k <= nmax using S(n+1,k+1) = S(n,k) + (k+1) S(n,k+1).

from __future__ import annotations

from itertools import product
from math import isqrt
from typing import Callable, Dict, Iterator, List, Optional, Sequence, Set, Tuple


def canonical_form(tup: Sequence[int]) -> Tuple[int, ...]:
    first: Dict[int, int] = {}
    out: List[int] = []
    for i, x in enumerate(tup):
        if x not in first:
            first[x] = i
        out.append(first[x])
    return tuple(out)


def enumerate_patterns(n: int) -> Iterator[Tuple[int, ...]]:
    if n == 0:
        yield ()
        return
    prefix: List[int] = []

    def extend(maximum: int) -> Iterator[Tuple[int, ...]]:
        if len(prefix) == n:
            yield canonical_form(prefix)
            return
        for label in range(maximum + 2):
            prefix.append(label)
            yield from extend(max(maximum, label))
            prefix.pop()

    yield from extend(-1)


def kernel_spectrum(
    arity: int,
    holds: Callable[[Tuple[int, ...]], bool],
    bound: int,
) -> Dict[Tuple[int, ...], Optional[Tuple[int, ...]]]:
    """Search all tuples with entries in [0, bound] and record which patterns occur.

    The search is organised by pattern rather than by tuple: for a pattern with k blocks
    only the k block-values are free, so the cost is
    sum over patterns of (bound+1)^{#blocks}, dominated by (bound+1)^arity but with a
    large saving on the degenerate patterns.  Returns a dictionary mapping every pattern
    of the given arity to a witnessing solution, or None if none was found in range.

    A negative entry is evidence, not proof: the arithmetic exclusions (for instance that
    the equal-legs pattern never occurs for x^p + y^p = z^p with p >= 2) require the
    valuation arguments of the accompanying theory.
    """
    result: Dict[Tuple[int, ...], Optional[Tuple[int, ...]]] = {}
    for pattern in enumerate_patterns(arity):
        labels = sorted(set(pattern))
        witness: Optional[Tuple[int, ...]] = None
        for values in product(range(bound + 1), repeat=len(labels)):
            if len(set(values)) != len(values):
                continue  # distinct blocks must carry distinct values
            assignment = dict(zip(labels, values))
            candidate = tuple(assignment[label] for label in pattern)
            if holds(candidate):
                witness = candidate
                break
        result[pattern] = witness
    return result


def pythagorean(t: Tuple[int, ...]) -> bool:
    return t[0] ** 2 + t[1] ** 2 == t[2] ** 2


def fermat(p: int) -> Callable[[Tuple[int, ...]], bool]:
    def holds(t: Tuple[int, ...]) -> bool:
        return t[0] ** p + t[1] ** p == t[2] ** p

    return holds


def equal_legs_dimension(k: int, bound: int = 500) -> Optional[Tuple[int, int]]:
    """Solve k a^2 = y^2 with a != 0; solvable exactly when k is a perfect square."""
    for a in range(1, bound + 1):
        s = k * a * a
        y = isqrt(s)
        if y * y == s:
            return a, y
    return None

# Kernel Patterns: the Shape of Sameness

> **What you will learn.** How the record of *which positions in a list agree* is a complete
> invariant for renaming the list's symbols; why counting those records produces the Bell numbers
> $1, 1, 2, 5, 15, 52, 203, \dots$; how the same picture proves Touchard's congruence
> $B_{p+n} \equiv B_{n+1} + B_n \pmod p$; and how attaching the invariant to
> $x^p + y^p = z^p$ turns Fermat's Last Theorem into a statement about the size of a
> five-element set.

---

## 1. Erase the symbols, keep the sameness

Here is a list: $(\text{red}, \text{blue}, \text{green}, \text{red}, \text{blue})$. Now here is
another: $(7, 4, 9, 7, 4)$. They share no entries at all, yet they are, in a precise sense, *the
same list*: rename $\text{red} \mapsto 7$, $\text{blue} \mapsto 4$, $\text{green} \mapsto 9$ and
one becomes the other.

What is preserved by such a renaming? Exactly the record of **which positions carry equal
entries**. Call that record the **kernel**, or **equality pattern**, of the list. Formally, the
kernel of a tuple $f = (f_0, \dots, f_{n-1})$ is the equivalence relation
$$i \sim j \iff f_i = f_j$$
on the set of positions, and equivalently the partition of positions into blocks.

To make this concrete rather than abstract, we label each block by its earliest position:

$$\mathrm{canon}(f)_i \;=\; \min\{\, j : f_j = f_i \,\}.$$

Play with it. Type any two lists into the laboratory below and watch the colours — positions
sharing a colour share an entry — and the verdict beneath them.

{{interactive_demo:0}}

<details>
<summary><b>The theorem behind the verdict (click to reveal)</b></summary>

**Completeness Theorem.** *Let $f, g$ be $n$-tuples with entries in a finite set $B$. There is a
permutation $\sigma$ of $B$ with $\sigma \circ f = g$ if and only if $f$ and $g$ have the same
equality pattern, i.e. $f_i = f_j \iff g_i = g_j$ for all $i,j$; equivalently, if and only if
$\mathrm{canon}(f) = \mathrm{canon}(g)$.*

*Proof.* ($\Rightarrow$) A permutation is injective, so it neither merges distinct entries nor
splits equal ones; the pattern is unchanged.

($\Leftarrow$) Assume the patterns agree. Define $e$ on the image of $f$ by choosing, for each
value $x$ taken by $f$, some position $i$ with $f_i = x$, and setting $e(x) = g_i$. The
hypothesis makes this independent of which position we chose: if $f_i = f_{i'}$ then $g_i =
g_{i'}$. The mirror-image construction from $\mathrm{im}(g)$ back to $\mathrm{im}(f)$ is inverse
to it, so $e$ is a bijection between the two images. Since $B$ is finite, the complements of the
images have the same size, so $e$ extends to a permutation $\sigma$ of all of $B$; and
$\sigma(f_i) = g_i$ for every $i$ by construction. $\blacksquare$

Note where finiteness enters: only in the extension step. This is the standard back-and-forth
subtlety, and it is why the theorem is stated over a finite alphabet.
</details>

The practical payoff is immediate: deciding whether two tuples are related by a renaming costs a
single linear scan, instead of a search through all $|B|!$ permutations.

{{algorithm:0}}

---

## 2. Counting the patterns: enter the Bell numbers

How many patterns of length $n$ are there? Patterns are exactly the *restricted growth strings*:
sequences starting at $0$ in which each entry is at most one more than the maximum so far. That
description makes them easy to generate without waste.

{{algorithm:1}}

Run it and the counts are $1, 1, 2, 5, 15, 52, 203, 877, 4140, \dots$ — the **Bell numbers**,
which count set partitions and which are usually *defined* by the recursion
$$B_{n+1} \;=\; \sum_{i=0}^{n} \binom{n}{i} B_{n-i}.$$

<details>
<summary><b>Why the two sequences must coincide, in four steps</b></summary>

1. **Patterns are equivalence relations.** Send $p$ to the relation $i \sim j \iff p_i = p_j$;
   recover $p$ by labelling each class by its least element. Bijection.
2. **Only the size matters.** A bijection of index sets carries equivalence relations to
   equivalence relations, so the count depends only on $n$.
3. **The adjoined point.** Let $I^+ = I \sqcup \{\star\}$. An equivalence relation on $I^+$ is the
   same data as a subset $s \subseteq I$ — the ordinary points sharing $\star$'s block — together
   with an equivalence relation on $I \setminus s$. Gluing and restricting are mutually inverse.
   Hence $K(I^+) = \sum_{s \subseteq I} K(I \setminus s)$.
4. **Regroup by size.** There are $\binom{n}{k}$ subsets of size $k$, so
   $K(n+1) = \sum_k \binom{n}{k} K(n-k)$ — the Bell recursion. Strong induction finishes it.

Read more on the sequence itself at [OEIS A000110](https://oeis.org/A000110).
</details>

## 3. Refining by block count: the Stirling triangle

Split the patterns of length $n$ by their number of blocks $k$, and call the count $S(n,k)$ —
the **Stirling numbers of the second kind**, here *defined* combinatorially rather than by a
formula. Almost everything classical about them follows from a single case split.

Click any cell of the triangle below to see the recursion that builds it, and use the second
panel to test Touchard's congruence for yourself.

{{interactive_demo:1}}

<details>
<summary><b>The recursion, and the closed forms it yields</b></summary>

**Recursion.** $S(n+1,k+1) = S(n,k) + (k+1)\,S(n,k+1)$.

*Proof.* Look at the last position of a pattern of length $n+1$ with $k+1$ blocks. Either it is a
block on its own — delete it and get a pattern of length $n$ with $k$ blocks, bijectively — or it
joins one of the $k+1$ existing blocks, which is a $(k+1)$-to-one correspondence with patterns of
length $n$ with $k+1$ blocks. $\blacksquare$

**Closed forms**, all proved by induction from the recursion:
$$S(n+1,2) = 2^n - 1, \qquad S(n+1,n) = \binom{n+1}{2}, \qquad
S(n+2,n) = \binom{n+2}{3} + 3\binom{n+2}{4},$$
$$6S(n,3) = 3^n - 3\cdot 2^n + 3, \quad 24S(n,4) = 4^n - 4\cdot 3^n + 6\cdot 2^n - 4,$$
$$120S(n,5) = 5^n - 5\cdot 4^n + 10\cdot 3^n - 10\cdot 2^n + 5.$$

Summing the resulting rows gives Bell numbers without enumerating anything:
$B_6 = 203$, $B_7 = 877$, $B_8 = 4140$.
</details>

## 4. Fibres, falling factorials, and how much symmetry buys you

Fix a pattern with $k$ blocks and an alphabet of $m$ letters. How many tuples realise that
pattern? You must choose one letter per block, all distinct: $m(m-1)\cdots(m-k+1) =
m^{\underline{k}}$ ways. Summing over all patterns partitions the $m^n$ tuples and gives the
**falling-factorial expansion**
$$m^n \;=\; \sum_{k} S(n,k)\, m^{\underline{k}},$$
while restricting to $m = k$ counts surjections: there are $k!\,S(n,k)$ maps from $n$ points
*onto* $k$ points.

The same fibre count answers a practical question: how much compression does the invariant give?
Over an alphabet of $m$ letters the number of orbits is
$$\sum_{k \le m} S(n,k),$$
which saturates at the Bell number $B_n$ precisely when $m \ge n$ — because a tuple over fewer
than $n$ letters can never have all entries distinct.

## 5. A congruence out of pure symmetry

Here is the most surprising consequence, and it costs one idea.

**Touchard's Congruence.** *For every prime $p$ and every $n \ge 0$,*
$$B_{p+n} \equiv B_{n+1} + B_n \pmod p.$$

<details>
<summary><b>The whole proof in one paragraph</b></summary>

Index a set by $\mathbb{Z}/p$ together with $n$ spectator points, and let the cyclic group of
order $p$ rotate the first part while fixing the spectators. It thereby acts on the $B_{p+n}$
partitions of the whole index set. For a group of prime order, every orbit has size $1$ or $p$,
so the total is congruent mod $p$ to the number of **fixed** partitions. Classify those by the
block of the cyclic point $0$: if that block contains another cyclic point $d$, invariance under
rotation by $d$ plus chaining (using that $d$ generates $\mathbb{Z}/p$) collapses the whole cycle
into one block, and what remains is a partition of the $n$ spectators together with that one
extra block — a partition of $n+1$ things, so $B_{n+1}$ of them. Otherwise every cyclic point is
a singleton and we are left with an arbitrary partition of the spectators, $B_n$ of them. Total:
$B_{n+1} + B_n$. $\blacksquare$

Setting $n = 0$ gives the classical $B_p \equiv 2 \pmod p$; e.g. $B_7 = 877 = 7 \cdot 125 + 2$.
Setting $p = 5$, $n = 3$ gives $5 \mid B_8$, and indeed $4140 = 5 \cdot 828$.
</details>

The same style of argument — an explicit injection between sets of partitions — gives the growth
laws: appending a fresh singleton block shows $B_n < B_{n+1}$ for $n \ge 1$, and laying two
partitions side by side on a disjoint union shows
$$B_m B_n < B_{m+n} \quad (m, n \ge 1),$$
strictly, because the all-in-one-block partition straddles the two halves and is missed by the
injection. Iterating gives $B_n^k \le B_{nk}$, so $2^k \le B_{2k}$: the Bell numbers outrun every
exponential.

## 6. Turning the invariant on arithmetic

Now the twist. Take any Diophantine equation in $n$ unknowns and ask which of the $B_n$ patterns
its solutions realise. Call that set of patterns the **kernel spectrum** of the equation: a
finite, purely combinatorial fingerprint of an infinite arithmetic object.

For triples there are $B_3 = 5$ patterns. Explore what each equation does with them:

{{interactive_demo:2}}

**Pythagoras.** Exactly four of the five patterns are realised by $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$ over the
natural numbers: $(3,4,5)$ gives the discrete pattern, and $(0,1,1)$, $(1,0,1)$, $(0,0,0)$ give
the degenerate ones. The single missing pattern is *equal legs, distinct hypotenuse*.

<details>
<summary><b>Why equal legs are impossible — and why they return in dimension four</b></summary>

**Square-Multiplier Lemma.** *If $ka^2 = c^2$ with $a \ne 0$, then $k$ is a perfect square.*

*Proof.* Divide $a$ and $c$ by $g = \gcd(a,c)$ to get coprime $a', c'$ with $ka'^2 = c'^2$. Then
$a'^2$ divides $c'^2$ while being coprime to it, so $a' = 1$ and $k = c'^2$. $\blacksquare$

Equal legs would mean $2a^2 = c^2$, and $2$ is not a square: blocked. But the lemma is an
*equivalence*, so for the $k$-dimensional equation $x_1^2 + \dots + x_k^2 = y^2$ the equal-legs
configuration exists **iff $k$ is a perfect square**. Blocked at $k = 2, 3$; realised at $k = 4$
by $1^2+1^2+1^2+1^2 = 2^2$. The missing pattern is a fact about dimension two, not about the
invariant.
</details>

**Fermat.** For $x^p + y^p = z^p$ with $p \ge 2$, the equal-legs pattern is blocked for *every*
exponent (compare the power of $2$ on both sides of $2a^p = c^p$: you get $p \mid 1$), and the
three degenerate patterns always occur. So only one pattern's fate is undecided — the discrete
one — and it is realised exactly when the equation has a solution in positive integers.

> **Kernel-Theoretic Fermat's Last Theorem.** For $p \ge 2$, the equation $x^p + y^p = z^p$
> realises exactly three of the five patterns of a triple if and only if it has no positive
> solution, and exactly four otherwise. At $p = 2$ the count is four; for $p \ge 3$ it is three.
> At $p = 1$ all five occur, since $1 + 1 = 2$ has equal legs.

  | .cubic     => fun n => n * n * n

  cases n with

  | succ m => nlinarith

  cases n with

/-!
# Generalized Midy's Theorem for Prime Reciprocals

This file distills the `2^m` framing of `HalfPeriodDigitSum.digitSum_half_period`
into its structural core: the only thing the arithmetic hypotheses ever buy us is
that the period length `l = ord_p(b)` is **even**. Whenever that holds, the
base-`b` digit sum of one full period of `1/p` equals `(b-1)·(l/2)`.

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
Hypothesis: the `2^m`/`p ≡ 1 [MOD 2^(m+1)]` conditions are a proxy for "the period
is even"; the true theorem needs only evenness of the multiplicative order.
Experiment: re-derived the digit-sum value from `Even l` alone.
Analysis: the square-root argument `b^(l/2) = -1` in the field `ZMod p` is the sole
mechanism; the number-theoretic input is exactly `Even (ord_p b)`. This explains
*why* Midy-style theorems always pair the two halves of a period.
Critique: `l` must be positive; in `ZMod p` (finite, `p` prime) the order of a unit
is automatically positive, so `Even l` gives `l ≥ 2`, hence `l/2 ≥ 1`.
Synthesis: `digitSum_half_period` is recovered as the special case where evenness
comes from `p ≡ 1 [MOD 2^(m+1)]`.
-/

namespace HalfPeriodDigitSum

open Nat

/-
**Generalized Midy's theorem.** For a prime `p ≥ 3`, base `b ≥ 2` with `p ∤ b`,
if the multiplicative order `l` of `b` mod `p` is even, then the base-`b` digit sum
of one full period of `1/p` (the digits of `(b^l - 1)/p`) equals `(b-1)·(l/2)`.
-/
theorem digitSum_midy_even
    (p b l : ℕ) (hp : p.Prime) (hp3 : 3 ≤ p) (hb : 2 ≤ b) (hpb : ¬ p ∣ b)
    (hord : orderOf ((b : ZMod p)) = l) (hl : Even l) :
    dsum b ((b ^ l - 1) / p) = (b - 1) * (l / 2) := by
  -- Let $h := l/2$. Then $l = 2h$.
  obtain ⟨h, rfl⟩ : ∃ h, l = 2 * h := even_iff_two_dvd.mp hl;
  -- From `x^h = -1`, `((b^h + 1 : ℕ) : ZMod p) = 0`, so `p ∣ b^h + 1` by `ZMod.natCast_eq_zero_iff`.
  have h_div : p ∣ b ^ h + 1 := by
    haveI := Fact.mk hp; simp_all +decide [ ← ZMod.natCast_eq_zero_iff ] ;
    have := pow_orderOf_eq_one ( b : ZMod p ) ; simp_all +decide [ pow_mul' ] ;
    cases this <;> simp_all +decide;
    have := orderOf_dvd_iff_pow_eq_one.mpr ‹_›; simp_all +decide [ Nat.dvd_iff_mod_eq_zero ] ;
    rcases h with ( _ | _ | h ) <;> simp_all +decide [ Nat.mod_eq_of_lt ];
    exact False.elim <| hord <| isOfFinOrder_iff_pow_eq_one.mpr ⟨ p - 1, Nat.sub_pos_of_lt hp.one_lt, by rw [ ZMod.pow_card_sub_one_eq_one hpb ] ⟩;
  -- Let `k := (b^h+1)/p`, giving `p*k = b^h+1`.
  obtain ⟨k, hk⟩ : ∃ k, b ^ h + 1 = p * k := h_div
  have hk_bounds : 1 ≤ k ∧ k ≤ b ^ h - 1 := by
    exact ⟨ by nlinarith [ pow_pos ( zero_lt_two.trans_le hb ) h ], Nat.le_sub_one_of_lt <| by nlinarith [ pow_pos ( zero_lt_two.trans_le hb ) h ] ⟩;
  -- Then `b^(2h) - 1` = (b^h-1)*(b^h+1) = p*(k*(b^h-1)), so `(b^(2h)-1)/p = k*(b^h-1)`.
  have h_div : (b ^ (2 * h) - 1) / p = k * (b ^ h - 1) := by
    exact Nat.div_eq_of_eq_mul_left hp.pos ( by zify at *; cases b <;> cases h <;> norm_num [ pow_mul' ] at * ; nlinarith );
  rw [ h_div, dsum_midy b h k hb hk_bounds.1 hk_bounds.2 ] ; norm_num

end HalfPeriodDigitSum",

/-!
# The two-block column of the Stirling triangle

We compute in closed form the number of kernel patterns of length `n + 1` with exactly two
blocks:

`KernelPattern.stirling2_two : stirling2 (n + 1) 2 = 2 ^ n - 1`.

The proof is a bijection with the family of subsets of `Fin (n+1)` that contain `0` and are
not everything: such a subset is the block of `0`, and the pattern is recovered as the
canonical form of its indicator tuple.  The auxiliary lemma
`KernelPattern.card_image_canon` (the canonical form has exactly as many values as the tuple
it comes from) is of independent interest.
-/

open Finset

namespace KernelPattern

variable {n : ℕ} {α : Type*} [DecidableEq α]

/-- The canonical form of a tuple takes exactly as many values as the tuple itself. -/
theorem card_image_canon (f : Fin n → α) :
    (univ.image (canon f)).card = (univ.image f).card := by
  refine Finset.card_bij (fun x _ => f x) ?_ ?_ ?_
  · intro x _
    exact Finset.mem_image_of_mem f (Finset.mem_univ x)
  · intro x hx y hy hxy
    simp only [Finset.mem_image, Finset.mem_univ, true_and] at hx hy
    obtain ⟨a, rfl⟩ := hx
    obtain ⟨b, rfl⟩ := hy
    have := (eq_iff_canon_eq f _ _).1 hxy
    rwa [canon_canon_apply, canon_canon_apply] at this
  · intro y hy
    simp only [Finset.mem_image, Finset.mem_univ, true_and] at hy
    obtain ⟨a, rfl⟩ := hy
    exact ⟨canon f a, Finset.mem_image_of_mem _ (Finset.mem_univ a), apply_canon f a⟩

/-- The block of the index `0` in a pattern. -/
def blockSet (p : Fin (n + 1) → Fin (n + 1)) : Finset (Fin (n + 1)) :=
  univ.filter (fun i => p i = 0)

/-- The pattern attached to a subset: the canonical form of its indicator tuple. -/
def patternOfSet (s : Finset (Fin (n + 1))) : Fin (n + 1) → Fin (n + 1) :=
  canon (fun i => decide (i ∈ s))

theorem patternOfSet_mem_patterns (s : Finset (Fin (n + 1))) :
    patternOfSet s ∈ Patterns (n + 1) := canon_mem_patterns _

theorem apply_zero_of_mem_patterns {p : Fin (n + 1) → Fin (n + 1)} (hp : p ∈ Patterns (n + 1)) :
    p 0 = 0 := by
  have h := canon_le_self p 0
  rw [mem_patterns_iff.1 hp] at h
  simpa using Fin.le_zero_iff.1 h

    blockSet (patternOfSet s) = s := by

  simp only [blockSet, Finset.mem_filter, Finset.mem_univ, true_and, patternOfSet]

  · intro hi

    have hval : decide ((canon (fun i => decide (i ∈ s)) i) ∈ s) = decide (i ∈ s) :=
      apply_canon (fun i => decide (i ∈ s)) i
    rw [hi] at hval

  · intro hi
    have hle : canon (fun i => decide (i ∈ s)) i ≤ 0 :=

def twoBlockSets (n : ℕ) : Finset (Finset (Fin (n + 1))) :=

    simp only [twoBlockSets, Finset.coe_filter, Set.mem_setOf_eq, Finset.mem_univ,

    simp only [twoBlockSets, Finset.coe_filter, Set.mem_setOf_eq, Finset.mem_univ,

    exact blockSet_patternOfSet hs.1

  have h_gcd_pos : 0 < Nat.gcd n α := Nat.gcd_pos_of_pos_left α hn

    by_contra h_ne
    have h_lt : Nat.gcd n α < α := lt_of_le_of_ne h_gcd_le h_ne

import Computation.FactorialNumberSystem

/-!
# Sorting: decision-tree entropy, reversible history, and Landauer work

Sorting distinct inputs has `n!` possible orderings.  This chapter separates three
quantities that are often conflated:

* the height of a binary comparison tree;
* the information erased by a many-to-one sorting map;
* the history space required to make that map reversible.

The same factorial controls all three, but raw comparison count does not itself measure
thermodynamic work: redundant comparisons may be inserted without changing the computed
map or its erased information.
-/

open Function

namespace SortingEntropyWork

/-- The shape of a binary comparison tree. -/
inductive ComparisonTree where
  | leaf : ComparisonTree
  | branch : ComparisonTree → ComparisonTree → ComparisonTree

namespace ComparisonTree

/-- Number of terminal transcripts. -/
def leaves : ComparisonTree → ℕ
  | leaf => 1
  | branch l r => leaves l + leaves r

/-- Worst-case number of comparisons. -/
def height : ComparisonTree → ℕ
  | leaf => 0
  | branch l r => 1 + max (height l) (height r)

/-- Insert `r` redundant comparison levels above a tree. -/
def pad : ℕ → ComparisonTree → ComparisonTree
  | 0, t => t
  | r + 1, t => branch (pad r t) (pad r t)

/-
A binary tree of height `h` has at most `2^h` terminal transcripts.
-/
theorem leaves_le_two_pow_height (t : ComparisonTree) :
    leaves t ≤ 2 ^ height t := by
      induction' t with l r ihl ihr;
      · decide +revert;
      · refine le_trans ( add_le_add ihl ihr ) ?_;
        simp +arith +decide [ ComparisonTree.height ];
        cases max_cases l.height r.height <;> simp_all +decide [ pow_add ];
        · linarith [ pow_le_pow_right₀ ( by decide : 1 ≤ 2 ) ‹_› ];
        · linarith [ pow_le_pow_right₀ ( by decide : 1 ≤ 2 ) ( by linarith : l.height ≤ r.height ) ]

/-
Padding adds an arbitrary number of comparisons to every execution.
-/
theorem height_pad (r : ℕ) (t : ComparisonTree) :
    height (pad r t) = r + height t := by
      induction' r with r ih generalizing t <;> simp_all +arith +decide;
      · rfl;
      · rw [ show pad ( r + 1 ) t = ComparisonTree.branch ( pad r t ) ( pad r t ) from rfl, ComparisonTree.height ] ; simp +arith +decide [ ih ]

/-
Padding never decreases the number of available transcripts.
-/
theorem leaves_le_pad (r : ℕ) (t : ComparisonTree) :
    leaves t ≤ leaves (pad r t) := by
      induction' r with r ih generalizing t;
      · rfl;
      · exact le_trans ( ih t ) ( by exact le_add_of_nonneg_left ( Nat.zero_le _ ) )

end ComparisonTree

/-- A comparison-tree shape can distinguish all orderings of `n` distinct items when it
has at least `n!` terminal transcripts. -/
def SortsOrderings (t : ComparisonTree) (n : ℕ) : Prop :=
  n.factorial ≤ t.leaves

/-
**Exact information lower bound.** Every comparison tree capable of distinguishing
all `n!` orderings has worst-case height at least `⌈log₂(n!)⌉`.
-/
theorem comparison_lower_bound (t : ComparisonTree) (n : ℕ)
    (hs : SortsOrderings t n) :
    Nat.clog 2 n.factorial ≤ t.height := by
      exact Nat.le_trans ( Nat.clog_mono_right _ <| show n.factorial ≤ 2 ^ t.height from hs.trans <|ComparisonTree.leaves_le_two_pow_height t ) ( by norm_num )

/-
Redundant comparisons can increase worst-case comparison count arbitrarily while
preserving the ability to sort the same inputs.
-/
theorem redundant_comparisons_preserve_sorting (t : ComparisonTree) (n r : ℕ)
    (hs : SortsOrderings t n) :
    SortsOrderings (t.pad r) n ∧ (t.pad r).height = r + t.height := by
      exact ⟨ le_trans hs ( ComparisonTree.leaves_le_pad r t ), ComparisonTree.height_pad r t ⟩

/-
**Three-way factorial synthesis.** A correct comparison tree obeys the entropy lower
bound; irreversible sorting erases exactly `log₂(n!)` bits; and every reversible
implementation needs at least `n!` history states.
-/
/-- The information erased by the sorting map, for *every* `n`: the hypothesis `1 ≤ n` of
`sorting_info_erased` is unnecessary, since for `n = 0` both sides are `0`. -/
theorem sorting_info_erased_all (n : ℕ) :
    infoErased (sortingFunction n) = Real.logb 2 n.factorial := by
  rcases Nat.eq_zero_or_pos n with rfl | hn
  · simp [infoErased, sortingFunction, Fintype.card_perm]
  · exact sorting_info_erased n hn

theorem factorial_controls_comparisons_entropy_and_history
    (t : ComparisonTree) (n : ℕ) (hs : SortsOrderings t n)
    (Aux : Type*) [Fintype Aux]
    (e : Equiv.Perm (Fin n) ≃ Unit × Aux)
    (hc : ∀ σ, (e σ).1 = sortingFunction n σ) :
    Nat.clog 2 n.factorial ≤ t.height ∧
    infoErased (sortingFunction n) = Real.logb 2 n.factorial ∧
    n.factorial ≤ Fintype.card Aux := by
      refine' ⟨ comparison_lower_bound t n hs, _, _ ⟩;
      · exact sorting_info_erased_all n
      · convert sorting_history_lower_bound n Aux e hc using 1;
        simp +decide [ Fintype.card_perm ]

/-
**Exact Landauer scale for sorting.** With natural logarithms, erasing the unknown
input permutation costs `kT · log(n!)`.  The factor `log 2` in the per-bit cost cancels
the change of base in `log₂(n!)`.
-/
theorem sorting_landauer_gap_exact (n : ℕ) (kT : ℝ) :
    landauerGap (sortingFunction n) kT = kT * Real.log n.factorial := by
      have h2 : Real.log 2 ≠ 0 := ne_of_gt (Real.log_pos (by norm_num))
      unfold landauerGap landauerCost
      rw [sorting_info_erased_all, Real.logb]
      field_simp

/-
The Landauer work assigned to irreversible sorting is unchanged when redundant
comparison levels are inserted.  Consequently, comparison count alone cannot equal
logical-erasure work without an additional physical model for how comparisons are reset.
-/
theorem padding_changes_comparisons_not_landauer_work
    (t : ComparisonTree) (n r : ℕ) (hs : SortsOrderings t n) (kT : ℝ) :
    SortsOrderings (t.pad r) n ∧
    (t.pad r).height = r + t.height ∧
    landauerGap (sortingFunction n) kT = landauerGap (sortingFunction n) kT := by
      exact ⟨ redundant_comparisons_preserve_sorting t n r hs |>.1, redundant_comparisons_preserve_sorting t n r hs |>.2, rfl ⟩

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
-- Hypothesis: A single factorial invariant should link decision-tree complexity,
-- reversible history, and thermodynamic erasure, while exposing the proposed law
-- “one comparison costs one bit” as too coarse.
-- Experiment: Small factorials and their binary ceilings were tabulated separately.
-- Padding a tree by duplicating both branches raises every path length while preserving
-- its suitability for the same sorting problem.
-- Analysis: The lower bound is combinatorial: `n! ≤ leaves ≤ 2^height`.  The thermodynamic
-- statement is instead a property of the computed many-to-one map.  Reversibility restores
-- the missing permutation as an auxiliary history with at least `n!` states.
-- Critique: `SortsOrderings` records transcript capacity, not comparison semantics, so it
-- gives a necessary lower bound rather than a full correctness specification.  Moreover,
-- mergesort does not always use exactly `log₂(n!)` comparisons, and bubble sort does not
-- erase one independent bit per comparison.  The padding theorem gives a structural
-- counterexample to identifying raw comparison count with Landauer work.
-- Synthesis: The surviving claim is a three-way lower-bound principle.  Factorial entropy
-- constrains comparison depth and reversible history, whereas actual dissipation depends
-- on which information is eventually erased and on the physical implementation.
-- !-- end Lab Notes -- !--

end SortingEntropyWork",

# The Fourier transform as the Wedderburn decomposition of `ℂ[G]`

For a finite abelian group `G`, the convolution algebra `ℂ[G] = AddMonoidAlgebra ℂ G` is
isomorphic, as a `ℂ`-algebra, to the algebra of *all* functions on the Pontryagin dual
`AddChar G ℂ` with pointwise multiplication.  This is the complete Wedderburn/Artin
decomposition of the group algebra in the abelian case: `ℂ[G] ≅ ℂ^{|G|}`, with the isomorphism
given by evaluating at characters, i.e. by the Fourier transform.

Main results:

* `FourierFA.evalHom_apply` : the evaluation-at-characters algebra map is `a ↦ (ψ ↦ ∑ₓ a x ψ x)`.
* `FourierFA.evalHom_eq_dft` : it is the Fourier transform of this development, up to inverting
  the character.
* `FourierFA.fourierAlgEquiv` : the algebra isomorphism `ℂ[G] ≃ₐ[ℂ] (AddChar G ℂ → ℂ)`.
* `FourierFA.isReduced_addMonoidAlgebra` : consequently `ℂ[G]` has no nonzero nilpotents.
-/

import Mathlib
import Shared.FourierFiniteAbelian

open Finset ComplexConjugate

namespace FourierFA

variable {G : Type*} [AddCommGroup G] [Fintype G] [DecidableEq G]

/-- `x ↦ (ψ ↦ ψ x)`, as a monoid homomorphism from `Multiplicative G` to the algebra of
functions on the dual group. -/
noncomputable def charMonoidHom : Multiplicative G →* (AddChar G ℂ → ℂ) where
  toFun := fun x => fun ψ => ψ (Multiplicative.toAdd x)
  map_one' := by funext ψ; simp
  map_mul' := by
    intro x y
    funext ψ
    simp [AddChar.map_add_eq_mul]

/-- Evaluation at characters, as a `ℂ`-algebra map out of the group algebra. -/
noncomputable def evalHom : AddMonoidAlgebra ℂ G →ₐ[ℂ] (AddChar G ℂ → ℂ) :=
  AddMonoidAlgebra.lift ℂ (AddChar G ℂ → ℂ) G charMonoidHom

omit [DecidableEq G] in
theorem evalHom_apply (a : AddMonoidAlgebra ℂ G) (ψ : AddChar G ℂ) :
    evalHom a ψ = ∑ x : G, a x * ψ x := by
  rw [evalHom, AddMonoidAlgebra.lift_apply, Finsupp.sum_fintype _ _ (by intro x; simp)]
  rw [Finset.sum_apply]
  exact Finset.sum_congr rfl fun x _ => by simp [charMonoidHom]

omit [DecidableEq G] in
/-- Evaluation at characters is exactly the discrete Fourier transform, read at the inverse
character. -/
theorem evalHom_eq_dft (a : AddMonoidAlgebra ℂ G) (ψ : AddChar G ℂ) :
    evalHom a ψ = dft (⇑a) (-ψ) := by
  rw [evalHom_apply, dft]
  refine Finset.sum_congr rfl fun x _ => ?_
  have h : conj ((-ψ) x) = ψ x := by
    rw [AddChar.neg_apply', map_inv₀, ← AddChar.inv_apply_eq_conj ψ x, inv_inv]
  rw [h]
  ring

theorem evalHom_bijective :
    Function.Bijective (evalHom : AddMonoidAlgebra ℂ G → (AddChar G ℂ → ℂ)) := by
  constructor
  · intro a b hab
    have h : dft (⇑a) = dft (⇑b) := by
      funext ψ
      have := congrFun hab (-ψ)
      rw [evalHom_eq_dft, evalHom_eq_dft, neg_neg] at this
      exact this
    exact Finsupp.ext (fun x => congrFun (dft_injective h) x)
  · intro F
    refine ⟨Finsupp.equivFunOnFinite.symm (idft (fun ψ => F (-ψ))), ?_⟩
    funext ψ
    have hcoe : ⇑(Finsupp.equivFunOnFinite.symm (idft (fun ψ => F (-ψ))))
        = idft (fun ψ => F (-ψ)) := rfl
    rw [evalHom_eq_dft, hcoe, idft_inversion (fun ψ => F (-ψ))]
    simp

/-- **Wedderburn decomposition of the complex group algebra of a finite abelian group**:
`ℂ[G]` is isomorphic, as a `ℂ`-algebra, to the algebra of functions on the dual group,
the isomorphism being the Fourier transform. -/
noncomputable def fourierAlgEquiv : AddMonoidAlgebra ℂ G ≃ₐ[ℂ] (AddChar G ℂ → ℂ) :=
  AlgEquiv.ofBijective evalHom evalHom_bijective

@[simp] theorem fourierAlgEquiv_apply (a : AddMonoidAlgebra ℂ G) (ψ : AddChar G ℂ) :
    fourierAlgEquiv a ψ = ∑ x : G, a x * ψ x := evalHom_apply a ψ

/-- Since it is isomorphic to a product of copies of `ℂ`, the group algebra of a finite abelian
group has no nonzero nilpotent elements. -/
theorem isReduced_addMonoidAlgebra : IsReduced (AddMonoidAlgebra ℂ G) := by
  constructor
  intro a ha
  have h1 : IsNilpotent (fourierAlgEquiv a) := ha.map fourierAlgEquiv
  have h2 : fourierAlgEquiv a = 0 := IsReduced.eq_zero _ h1
  exact fourierAlgEquiv.injective (by rw [h2, map_zero])

end FourierFA",

This chapter connects three structures that are usually treated separately:
the strong-divisibility law of the Fibonacci sequence, gcd aggregation over a
finite family, and primitive prime divisors at prime indices.  The resulting
synchronization theorem says that, for every prime index `q ≥ 13`, one can find

at one index to a global description of all later appearances of the divisor.

  sequence; (2) exact apparition at prime Fibonacci indices; (3) finite-family

  description at arbitrary composite indices; (7) an elliptic-divisibility

  either `1` or `q`.

  pattern is that a binary strong-divisibility identity automatically preserves
  finite meets.  Primitive divisibility at a prime index then determines the
  complete infinite divisibility locus, not merely the first occurrence.

  collapse of divisors of `q`.  Empty finite sets are not hidden exceptions.
  The proofs use induction, contradiction, and gcd divisibility rather than a
  finite decision procedure.

  as a uniform statement over all finite index families, making the recurrence

/-- Finite gcds commute with the Fibonacci map.  Thus the binary strong
Divisibility identity extends to every finite family of indices. -/
theorem finset_gcd_fib (s : Finset ℕ) :

  | empty => simp

      exact Fib_gcd_identity a (s.gcd id)

Divides the Fibonacci value at the gcd of that family. -/
theorem dvd_fib_finset_gcd_iff (p : ℕ) (s : Finset ℕ) :

/-!
# End-to-end collision factoring, and the two barriers it must pass

This file glues the two halves of the story together:

and it isolates a second, independent obstruction that the naive "cost = number
of tuples" accounting hides.

**Barrier 1 (counting).**  A guaranteed `r`-SUM collision needs more than `p`
tuples, hence more than `√N` work at any arity `r`.

**Barrier 2 (amplitude).**  A collision is *useful* only if the two colliding
tuples have different integer sums.  All `r`-tuples drawn from `A ⊆ [1, M]` have
sums in `[r, rM]`, so at most `rM - r + 1` distinct sums exist.  If `r * M < p`
then *every* modular collision is trivial (`all_collisions_trivial_of_small`)
and the scheme cannot factor at all, no matter how many tuples are inspected.
Thus the entries themselves must be of size `≥ p / r`, and the useful search
space is capped by `r * M`, not by `|A| ^ r`.

The master theorem `rsum_factoring_success` shows that once both barriers are
passed the scheme provably outputs the factor `p`.

Main results:

* `useful_collision_of_sumset_card_lt` — a sumset larger than `p` contains a
  nontrivial modular collision.
* `rsum_factoring_success` — end-to-end: it outputs `gcd = p`.
* `all_collisions_trivial_of_small` — the amplitude barrier.
* `sumset_card_le_amplitude` — the useful search space is at most `r * M`.
* `rsum_needs_both_barriers` — a successful scheme must satisfy `p ≤ r * M`
  *and* inspect more than `√N` tuples.
-/

namespace CollisionFactoring

open Finset ThreeSumReveal BirthdayHierarchy

/-! ## Nontrivial collisions come from a large *sumset* -/

/-- **Useful collision.**  If the set `T` of achieved sums has more than `p`
elements, two of them are distinct integers congruent modulo `p`. -/
theorem useful_collision_of_sumset_card_lt {p : ℕ} {T : Finset ℕ} (hp : 0 < p)
    (hT : p < T.card) : ∃ s ∈ T, ∃ t ∈ T, t < s ∧ p ∣ s - t := by
  obtain ⟨x, hx, y, hy, hne, hxy⟩ :=
    Finset.exists_ne_map_eq_of_card_lt_of_maps_to (t := Finset.range p)
      (by simpa using hT) (f := fun n => n % p)
      (fun n _ => Finset.mem_range.mpr (Nat.mod_lt _ hp))
  rcases lt_or_gt_of_ne hne with h | h
  · exact ⟨y, hy, x, hx, h, (Nat.modEq_iff_dvd' h.le).mp hxy⟩
  · exact ⟨x, hx, y, hy, h, (Nat.modEq_iff_dvd' h.le).mp hxy.symm⟩

/-! ## The set of sums of `r`-tuples -/

/-- All integer sums achieved by `r`-tuples over `A`. -/
noncomputable def sumSet (r : ℕ) (A : Finset ℕ) : Finset ℕ :=
  (tupleSpace r A).image (fun u => ∑ i, u i)

theorem mem_sumSet_le {r M : ℕ} {A : Finset ℕ} (hA : ∀ a ∈ A, a ≤ M)
    {s : ℕ} (hs : s ∈ sumSet r A) : s ≤ r * M := by
  simp only [sumSet, Finset.mem_image] at hs
  obtain ⟨u, hu, rfl⟩ := hs
  have hu' : ∀ i : Fin r, u i ∈ A := by
    simpa [tupleSpace, Fintype.mem_piFinset] using hu
  calc ∑ i, u i ≤ ∑ _i : Fin r, M := Finset.sum_le_sum (fun i _ => hA _ (hu' i))
    _ = r * M := by simp

/-- **Amplitude barrier.**  The number of distinct sums produced by `r`-tuples
over `A ⊆ [1, M]` is at most `r * M`, no matter how big `|A| ^ r` is. -/
theorem sumset_card_le_amplitude {r M : ℕ} {A : Finset ℕ} (hA : ∀ a ∈ A, a ≤ M) :
    (sumSet r A).card ≤ r * M + 1 := by
  have hsub : sumSet r A ⊆ Finset.range (r * M + 1) := by
    intro s hs
    exact Finset.mem_range.mpr (Nat.lt_succ_of_le (mem_sumSet_le hA hs))
  simpa using Finset.card_le_card hsub

/-- **Every collision is trivial when the entries are small.**  If `r * M < p`
then any two `r`-tuples over `A ⊆ [1, M]` with congruent sums modulo `p` have
*equal* integer sums, so the collision carries no arithmetic information: the
gcd step returns `N` or `1`, never a factor. -/
theorem all_collisions_trivial_of_small {p r M : ℕ} {A : Finset ℕ}
    (hA : ∀ a ∈ A, a ≤ M) (hsmall : r * M < p)
    {u v : Fin r → ℕ} (hu : u ∈ tupleSpace r A) (hv : v ∈ tupleSpace r A)
    (hcong : (∑ i, u i) % p = (∑ i, v i) % p) :
    (∑ i, u i) = ∑ i, v i := by
  have hus : (∑ i, u i) ∈ sumSet r A := Finset.mem_image_of_mem _ hu
  have hvs : (∑ i, v i) ∈ sumSet r A := Finset.mem_image_of_mem _ hv
  have h1 := mem_sumSet_le hA hus
  have h2 := mem_sumSet_le hA hvs
  rcases lt_trichotomy (∑ i, u i) (∑ i, v i) with h | h | h
  · exfalso
    have hd : p ∣ (∑ i, v i) - ∑ i, u i := (Nat.modEq_iff_dvd' h.le).mp hcong
    have hpos : 0 < (∑ i, v i) - ∑ i, u i := Nat.sub_pos_of_lt h
    have := Nat.le_of_dvd hpos hd
    omega
  · exact h
  · exfalso
    have hd : p ∣ (∑ i, u i) - ∑ i, v i := (Nat.modEq_iff_dvd' h.le).mp hcong.symm
    have hpos : 0 < (∑ i, u i) - ∑ i, v i := Nat.sub_pos_of_lt h
    have := Nat.le_of_dvd hpos hd
    omega

/-! ## End-to-end success -/

/-- **Master theorem: `r`-SUM collision factoring works once both barriers are

over `A` has more than `p` elements.  Then the search finds two tuple sums
`t < s` whose difference exposes `p`:  `gcd (s - t) N = p`. -/

    (hbig : p < (sumSet r A).card) :
    ∃ s ∈ sumSet r A, ∃ t ∈ sumSet r A, t < s ∧
      Nat.gcd (s - t) (p * q) = p := by
  obtain ⟨s, hs, t, ht, hts, hdvd⟩ :=
    useful_collision_of_sumset_card_lt hp.pos hbig
  refine ⟨s, hs, t, ht, hts, ?_⟩
  exact collision_gcd_reveal hp hq hts
    (lt_of_le_of_lt (mem_sumSet_le hA hs) hMN) hdvd

suffices to factor `N = p * q`. -/
theorem threeSum_factoring_success {p q M : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) (hq : q.Prime)
    {A : Finset ℕ} (hA : ∀ a ∈ A, a ≤ M) (hMN : 3 * M < p * q)
    (hbig : p < (sumSet 3 A).card) :

  rsum_factoring_success hp hq hA hMN hbig

/-- **Span barrier (arity- and structure-free).**  If every value produced by a
scheme lies in an interval of length `p` (i.e. `L ≤ x < L + p`), then congruent
values are equal: no useful collision exists.  This holds for *any* collision
scheme — sumset, 3SUM, `r`-SUM, or an evaluation scheme such as singular moduli
— because it constrains only the numerical values, not how they are produced.
Consequently the values themselves must span a range of size at least `p`, and
for `q ≤ p` at least `√N`. -/
theorem span_barrier {p L : ℕ} {T : Finset ℕ}
    (hT : ∀ x ∈ T, L ≤ x ∧ x < L + p) :
    ∀ s ∈ T, ∀ t ∈ T, s % p = t % p → s = t := by
  intro s hs t ht hst
  obtain ⟨hs1, hs2⟩ := hT s hs
  obtain ⟨ht1, ht2⟩ := hT t ht
  rcases lt_trichotomy s t with h | h | h
  · have hd : p ∣ t - s := (Nat.modEq_iff_dvd' h.le).mp hst
    have := Nat.le_of_dvd (Nat.sub_pos_of_lt h) hd
    omega
  · exact h
  · have hd : p ∣ s - t := (Nat.modEq_iff_dvd' h.le).mp hst.symm
    have := Nat.le_of_dvd (Nat.sub_pos_of_lt h) hd
    omega

/-- Contrapositive form: a useful (factor-revealing) collision forces the value
range to be at least `p`, hence at least `√N` when `q ≤ p`. -/
theorem span_ge_of_useful_collision {p s t : ℕ} (hts : t < s)
    (hdvd : p ∣ s - t) : p ≤ s - t :=
  Nat.le_of_dvd (Nat.sub_pos_of_lt hts) hdvd

  · have := sumset_card_le_amplitude (r := r) hA
    omega
  · have hcard : (sumSet r A).card ≤ (tupleSpace r A).card :=
      Finset.card_image_le
    have : p < A.card ^ r := by
      have := card_tupleSpace r A
      omega
    exact tuple_scheme_cost_gt_sqrt hqp this

  ⟨(rsum_needs_both_barriers hqp hA hbig).1, (rsum_needs_both_barriers hqp hA hbig).2⟩

Building on `Catalog.Shared.FourierFiniteAbelian` and `Catalog.Shared.FourierSubgroupDuality`,
this file records how the DFT interacts with the three basic symmetries of `G → ℂ`
(scaling, translation, modulation) and deduces a large family of functions attaining
equality in the Donoho–Stark uncertainty principle `|supp f| * |supp f̂| ≥ |G|`.

* `FourierFA.dft_transl` : `(f(· - a))^(ψ) = conj (ψ a) · f̂(ψ)` (translation ↦ modulation).
* `FourierFA.dft_modul` : `(χ · f)^(ψ) = f̂(ψ - χ)` (modulation ↦ translation in the dual).
* `FourierFA.IsExtremal` : the property `|supp f| * |supp f̂| = |G|`.
* `FourierFA.IsExtremal.smul`, `.transl`, `.modul` : the extremal functions form a set invariant
  under the three symmetries.

  `x ↦ c · χ x · 1_H (x - a)` (with `c ≠ 0`, `H` a subgroup) is extremal.
